segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 1970s in Europe were marked by a bold, angry and talented new generation making powerful, controversial films.
segments.text: The nineteen seventies in Europe were marked by a bold, angry and talented new generation making powerful, controversial films.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In the 1970s, the pantheon of established masters who had set the tone for Western European cinema in the postwar years began to discover that it was losing ground to a new generation of talented, ambitious filmmakers with ideas and attitudes of their own. In German cinema this happened relatively smoothly, since at the start of the decade there were few veterans of any standing. Elsewhere the transition was less peaceful, as some of the old masters - such as Luis Buñuel (1900-1983), Robert Bresson (1901-1999) and Ingmar Bergman (1918-2007) - were still at their peak.

segments.original: The screenplay of Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom is based on the work of the same title by the Marquis de Sade, who gave his name to the specific form of sexual perversion the film explores. Although the narrative differs from Sade's book in many respects, it still preserves its essence. The Marquis de Sade's project was partly political, aiming to satirize the dominant institutions of his time, above all the Catholic Church. Pasolini was also fervently anticlerical, but he ties Sodom directly to Italian history.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The film is set in Salò, a very short-lived republic where Mussolini established his last stronghold of resistance at the end of World War II. Pasolini was caught up in these events, and his brother was killed in Salò. In Pasolini's fantasy about this episode of the war, four fascist libertines have total power over a group of young, attractive prisoners of both sexes and subject them to a series of sexual tortures and humiliations. These are presented by the director in a series of coldly formal scenes that are curiously devoid of any erotic tension. Nor is there any intention of developing the characters: even the libertines are barely defined in terms of personality and seem to derive no real pleasure from their debauchery, while their victims are essentially anonymous, simply bodies to be abused and penetrated.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Pasolini's intention was to turn the unlimited use of power, taken to the most radical sexual degradation, into a metaphor for fascism itself, seen as a philosophy that worships power as an end in itself. There are other messages, however. One libertine is identified as a bishop and, at one point, two of the victims are subjected to a sort of wedding ceremony, although the consummation is interrupted by the libertines, who place their own bodies between the newlyweds. And, in a particularly notorious scene, a naked young woman is forced to eat excrement; Pasolini always argued that this was a metaphor for mass consumer capitalism and its production of junk food.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The obscenities the film presents have an undeniable power to shock; perhaps most disturbing is that, at this point in his career, Pasolini had at best an ambiguous attitude toward the body and sexuality. If the aim of pornography is to stimulate sexual desire, Sodom would not fit the definition, because its effect and, presumably, its purpose are to generate revulsion. Shortly after this radical and disturbing film was completed, and even before it was released, Pasolini was murdered. His film was persecuted or banned in many countries, and only after several decades did it become available to the general public in England and the United States.

segments.original: In December 2016, the controversy returned: a 2013 video resurfaced on social media and shocked Hollywood. "The sequence of the butter is an idea that I had with Marlon the day before shooting. I wanted Maria to react, to be humiliated," Bertolucci says. "I didn't want her to act the rage, I wanted her to feel the rage and humiliation," he added. In the United States the controversy grew, less than a year before the Weinstein case and the revelations about the sexual assaults suffered by several actresses. segments.original: One director who built his film career dealing with cases of state-inflicted justice was the Greek-born, naturalized French Costa-Gavras (b. 1933). In the 1970s he directed L'Aveu (The Confession, 1970), criticizing the communists in Prague in 1951, État de siège (State of Siege, 1972), targeting CIA involvement in Uruguay, and Section spéciale (Special Section, 1975), dealing with the Vichy government in France during the war.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Eclectic as he was, Louis Malle (1932-1995) moved easily between political and historical subjects and intimate family dramas. In Lacombe Lucien (1974), he confronted the delicate subject of French fascism during the Occupation, while in Le souffle au cœur (Murmur of the Heart, 1971) he shocked French society with his sympathetic treatment of mother-son incest. Marco Ferreri (1928-1997) alarmed the censors with his allegories of capitalist greed - sex and gluttonous extravagance in La Grande Bouffe (1973) and more excess with the elaborate La dernière femme (The Last Woman, 1976). But the scandal caused by these films did not compare with the furor surrounding Ultimo tango a Parigi (Last Tango in Paris, 1972), by Bernardo Bertolucci (b. 1940).

segments.original: Many of these films represented an open or implicit reaction to the rise of feminism. More authoritative statements came with the work of a number of Western European women directors in the 1970s. Anja Breien (b. 1940), from Norway, found success with the good-humored feminism of Hustruer (Wives, 1975). The melodrama of Italian films such as Il portiere di notte (The Night Porter, 1974), by Liliana Cavani (b. 1933), and Travolti da un insolito destino nell'azzurro mare d'agosto (Swept Away, 1974), by Lina Wertmüller (b. 1926), contrasted with the minimalism of French playwright Marguerite Duras (1914-1996) in films such as India Song (1975). Minimalism also influenced Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975), a study of bourgeois prostitution by Chantal Akerman (b. 1950). Several actresses turned to directing, among them Gunnel Lindblom (b. 1931) with her study of a dysfunctional Swedish family, ironically titled Summer Paradise (1976).
